utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two points about the witness list: The parties have been informed that Ante Marinovic will not now be called. He was on your list as the next witness but one, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is he postponed or is he out of the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Out of the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The remainder of witnesses for this short week are 92 bis witnesses plus two witnesses who are more substantial. If the Chamber will accept this as a practice, we would prefer to take the witness Stjepan Kljuc as near as maybe at the beginning of tomorrow morning however 92 bis witnesses we've got through, in order to make sure that he's disposed of this week; and similarly, we'd start to start B-127 as near as may be to the beginning of Wednesday so that those substantial witnesses can be got through and the 92 bis witnesses can be used to wrap around them or fill in as appropriate. If that seems an acceptable course, we'll plan on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll obviously consider that and do what is convenient to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me raise something. Mr. Groome last week asked us to deal with a number of Bosnia 92 bis witnesses who it was proposed to be called in the last two weeks, and he mentioned a list of nine priority witnesses. I have looked, over the weekend, at these statements, and I would propose that we deal with them tomorrow for oral argument. However, there are two missing statements in my binder, and I'll give you the numbers, and if the Prosecution want the statements dealt with, I would like those today. And the numbers are B-1704 and B-1010. As I say, I don't have those, and if you would supply them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry that that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon will be taking the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Witness C-1149. Your Honours, while we're waiting for the witness to enter, part of this witness's testimony will be about an agriculture centre found in the municipality of Zrenjanin in the Republic of Serbia. Zrenjanin can be seen on Exhibit 326, tab 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C-1149, you have been granted certain protective measures by the Trial Chamber, and today I will refer to you by your pseudonym C-1149. Would you be kind enough, please, to take a look at a piece of paper that's being shown to you now and just tell us, please, by answering yes or no, is that your name on the first line of that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, recently did you review your witness statement in the presence of an officer of this court and attest to its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you then sign the documentation, showing that you had attested your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have the following short summary of the witness's statement, Your Honours. In 1991, Witness C-1149 resided near Vukovar, Croatia. On the 19th of November, 1991, he and approximately 1.700 other mostly Croat men and boys were forcibly transported on buses from the Vukovar area to a camp in the Vojvodina region of the Republic of Serbia. Most of the prisoners were Croats, but about 10 per cent of them were Serbs or members of other nationalities. Witness C-1149's written statement describes how these men were forced at gunpoint by members of the JNA and paramilitaries to board buses near Vukovar, how they were beaten and verbally abused, and then transported to a camp outside the town of Zrenjanin in the Republic of Serbia at a farm known as Stajicevo. Witness C-1149 describes how the prisoners were brutally beaten upon their arrival at the camp and on a daily basis thereafter. Prisoners were held in a cattle shed with no access to toilet facilities nor water for bathing and were not given sufficient food or medical care. Your Honours, if I may, I have several questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's identify the exhibit and give it a number for the 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P500, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C-1149, in your written statement you describe how on 19 November 1991, Serb forces near Vukovar forced you and hundreds of other men and boys onto buses at gunpoint. Do you know what units or forces these Serbs belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: They were the JNA, the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any local paramilitary forces present as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you and the other detainees were being placed on the buses, did these soldiers and paramilitaries abuse the detainees verbally and physically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: They beat us. They threatened us, to kill us, some of us. They used the most dreadful verbal abuse and threats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you and the other detainees boarded the buses, who was inside the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Paramilitaries. Paramilitary men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "paramilitaries." Do you know the specific unit that these men belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: No. They didn't have insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know many of the people boarding these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I had lived with them and worked with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity or nationality of the people who you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any Serbs on those buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: There were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without mentioning your profession or the village where you lived, can you explain why there were Serb men placed onto the buses as well as non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Because they captured us. They didn't ask anyone their names or their ethnicity, they just rounded us up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the buses left the Vukovar area and crossed the Danube River into Vojvodina in the Republic of Serbia, did you hear anything on the bus's radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes. The radio was on in the buses, and we heard over the radio that our convoy was passing through Vojvodina and the people were calling for a lynch, and they threw stones at us as we passed through towns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the radio broadcaster describe the people who were on that convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: That they were killers, that 1.200 Ustashas who had killed Serb civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You describe in your written statement how prisoners were beaten upon their arrival at the camp in Stajicevo. Were Serb detainees beaten upon their arrival at the camp as well? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were the Serb detainees beaten as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Because for them, they were traitors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were the Serb detainees described as traitors, or why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Because they had stayed behind in their apartments and houses, and they had been with the Croats for three months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your written statement, you explain that the commander of the camp was Lieutenant Colonel Zivanovic from the military police. Was Lieutenant Colonel Zivanovic present when detainees were being beaten in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Lieutenant Colonel Zivanovic take any measures to stop these beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: He didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we move very briefly into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your written statement, you mention seven severely wounded detainees who were sent to the hospital in Zrenjanin, refused treatment, and then returned to the camp. Do you know the nationality of these seven men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told why they were refused treatment in the hospital in Zrenjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: That Serbia would not provide medicine to Ustashas and would not treat them medically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. C-1149, how long have you lived in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Since 1964.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came to study; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you got citizenship only in 1993, as far as I managed to see from your details.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the Republic of Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You lived in Vukovar from 1982?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you practised your profession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you've got any more questions along this line, in private session. Perhaps we'd better go into private session to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1149, I assume that you were not a member of any political party at that time in the former Yugoslavia, and you're not a member even now, or perhaps I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I've never been a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, during your stay, you maintained friendly ties and relations with many people in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Irrespective of their ethnic background; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said awhile ago that the people you worked with, socialised with were Croats, but from your statement I saw that some of them were Serbs too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had professional, correct relations, friendly relations with all, irrespective of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Irrespective of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in view of the fact that at the time you were a foreigner in a country where there were ethnic conflicts, how did you view these ethnic conflicts? What did you infer from that? What was actually going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Well, what was going on. We lived in peace and then the attack on Vukovar started and the siege of Vukovar. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this attack on Vukovar and the surrounding area start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: At first there were a lot of skirmishes, and on the 26th of August, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 24th [as interpreted] of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything, as an inhabitant of Vukovar, about any kind of pressures, violence - not to enumerate all these things - directed against the Serbs towards the end of 1990 and throughout 1991 when the attack was launched? Do you know anything about this? You lived in the area; you had many ties and relationships.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I know that after the 2nd of May, there was a barricade. I know that from Borovo Selo, Trpinja they prohibited workers from coming to work in Borovo factory. These were barricades set up by the Serb paramilitaries. Unfortunately, my colleagues who were ethnic Serbs left their jobs and did not return to the workplace after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did your colleagues not return to their workplace, those who were ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Well, that seemed to be the policy then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know anything about the violence that was directed against the Serbs in Vukovar at that time, that is to say in 1991, before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally don't know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked about this violence. Was there any -- As far as you knew, was there any violence directed at the Serbs? What is the truth of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was no, and I said where I was. And in the shelter where I lived for three months, there were about 15 Serb families with their children, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. During 1991, especially from the end of July, when you returned from Zagreb to Vukovar, did you notice that Serbs were leaving Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: A large number of them had already left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think they were leaving it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Well, probably it didn't suit them, the victory of the HDZ, that is, and the separation of Croatia from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from these opinions, you're saying that there weren't -- that there wasn't any violence directed at the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you hear about any of these things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Only over the Serb radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only over the Serb radio? You didn't hear anything from your friends - Croats, Serbs - who lived in Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- about the situation in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. 1149, you say that all men, together with members of the National Guards Corps, were boarded onto buses and that there were about 1.700 of you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on the basis of your experience and in your opinion, how many ZNGs were there in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: About 7 to 8 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those in uniform, they were about 300, is that right, in all? That's what you said a moment ago, about 300.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you assist me in finding out how you could distinguish between those who were in civilian clothing and those in uniform except that they all had weapons? What was the other distinguishing trait?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Some were in uniform whereas the others were in civilian clothes. That was the main difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were boarded onto the buses, no one could establish who amongst you were members of the National Guards Corps and who were civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: They separated the men -- men from 14 to 100 years of age. All men were boarded onto the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there someone of a hundred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes, there was, a patient who was in the camp and who was 90.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they took him too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they took Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: When they separated us, they didn't ask us what nationality we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's precisely what I want to establish. They knew that there were members of different ethnicities living there, and they didn't ask you what ethnicity you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: They thought they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Well, if they insulted all of us, saying that we were Ustashas and killers and that we would be liquidated --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did they call you killers if those 300 of them, as you say, didn't kill anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: They may have killed somebody in defence. They didn't attack anyone. They were in Borovo Naselje, and they were defending it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know anything at all about whether those units had killed anyone, committed any crimes, or anything like that due to which those people were furious?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I lived through the war. There was shooting. In war there is shooting, and there are victims, too, and casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is beyond dispute. But those citizens who were around you when you were being boarded onto the bus, were they furious? Were they cursing at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: They were not citizens. They were the military police, the JNA, the army, and paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did they treat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: They separated women and children to one side, men from 14 to old age to the other. They boarded the men onto buses, the women and children onto trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- okay. The women and children, I suppose nothing happened to them, but what happened to you who were transported to Stajicevo? You say you went to Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there? From what I heard you say, it was for 12 days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout that period, you performed your work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Stajicevo, did the army have jurisdiction over that centre or the military police only, only they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes, the army and the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see any representative of the authorities, even municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Only the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you see members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: In the camp. They beat us. And they welcomed us there. They were waiting for us when the buses arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the others stay in Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I think until the 15th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I don't know. I would like to ask you what happened to them. They were scattered across prisons in Serbia. Stajicevo as a place was destroyed as evidence. That agricultural estate no longer exists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's an agricultural estate. What is there to exist, to destroy there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: It used to be an agricultural estate, but it hadn't been in use for 15 years. There was no electricity, no water, no sewage, no glass. It hadn't been used at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any of those people, were they killed? Were they victimised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes, we were all victimised, but only one was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: He was shot at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he shot at and who shot at him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: If we are in a camp, then I don't know who could possibly shoot at us except the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did they shoot at that particular individual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I don't know. They told me personally that he wanted to escape and that's why they shot him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So out of 1.700 of you, one was killed, allegedly when trying to escape. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Only one was killed, but we all suffered beatings. I have injuries on my spine in the neck area from the beatings I got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: You say "Fine." It's not fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not saying that the fact that they beat you is fine, Mr. C-1149, I'm just saying fine in the context of your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant -- the lieutenant colonel, I think, was not mentioned in private session but in public session, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you are saying, I see that with Lieutenant Colonel Zivanovic, whom you mention as being the responsible person for that centre, that you had -- that you were on good terms with him. You communicated well with him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes, I was on good terms with him after I was mistreated all night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please describe that for me. It's not quite clear to me. Was there when you arrived there somebody mistreated you and then the next day, in the morning, you established good relations with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I think it right -- what is said in my statement is quite clear. The mistreatment started on the bus, and when we were getting off the bus there was two lines of policemen, soldiers, were beating us until we entered the stables. Then they continued beating us until the morning. And we doctors that were there, we had special treatment. We were given special treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the morning, you met the commander, Lieutenant Colonel Zivanovic? [redacted] He spoke to the lieutenant colonel and told him that I had treated both and that I had helped everyone and that I was a foreigner. He didn't know that until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Please, you explained that those people who had captured you beat you regardless of whether people were Serbs, Croats, or foreigners, regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that they considered you some kind of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I think a prisoner of war shouldn't be beaten and mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I also think that no one must beat or mistreat prisoners of war, but I'm just asking you, did they consider you prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But still they mistreated you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He, the lieutenant colonel, that same day permitted medical treatment to be given to all sick or wounded prisoners regardless of whether they were members of the National Guards Corps or other units, that everyone be treated without exception; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session and deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, since you lived for many years in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, you had occasion to see in other towns of the former Yugoslavia barracks, because they existed in the centres of many towns; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those barracks were tanks and cannon within the compound, that didn't come out into the street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about this time when the conflict broke out, I'm talking about peacetime.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: In peacetime certainly they were not in the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I was asking. Also, when soldiers walked the streets, they were not armed during their free time, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that guns and tanks in the Vinkovci barracks were within the barracks compound, weren't they, when they were shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Let me correct you first. I didn't mention Vinkovci. I didn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. live --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Vukovar, I meant Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: From the 2nd of May, when the massacre occurred in Borovo Selo, JNA tanks were in the towns. They patrolled Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid there's a misunderstanding. I'm talking about the months of July and August, before the conflict occurred. The cannon and the tanks were within the barracks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They never came out. There was no reason; there wasn't any military parade or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when the conflict broke out, when they were surrounded, they responded by opening fire from the barracks with cannon and tanks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Listen, now: You're telling your own story. You say surrounded. On the 2nd of May, not a single barracks was surrounded, in Vukovar or in Vinkovci. And what happened happened in Borovo Selo. From then on, the army patrolled the town and APCs in tanks. In tanks and APCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to make things clear. When the conflict occurred, you say that JNA soldiers opened fire from tanks and cannon from the barracks, whereas the barracks were surrounded by members of the ZNG. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: You're talking about ZNG members. There was the reserve police force. There were also volunteers who were defending their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about Croats.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes, Croats. Then how can somebody with an automatic rifle attack a barracks that has 300 tanks, or threaten it? You keep saying that the army was not attacking but it was only defending itself. That's not true. It can't be true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't say anything. I just asked you to explain things. I'm not claiming anything. I want to know whether you know if, among the soldiers within the barracks, there were any killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, if you can finish this witness before the adjournment, so much the better. We started a bit late, so we can sit on a bit late.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will do my best. Re-examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify one confusion, Witness C-1149. At one point in the transcript it appears that you say that you arrived in the camp on the 19th of December. Did you arrive in the camp on the 19th of December or the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: The 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what unit or institution Lieutenant Colonel Zivanovic belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: The military police of the JNA. The JNA military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Lieutenant Colonel Zivanovic have any subordinates working at the Stajicevo camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: I met two majors apart from others of lower rank. And at the interrogations there was also a major who interrogated me. As for the others, I don't know how many there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these majors also members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: The major who was the most active one, he was not from the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the first night in -- do you know which unit or institution that major belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the first night in the camp, did Serb detainees continue to suffer beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: After the first night, they were beaten less because they formed a separate group. But when they went for interrogation, they were also beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the first night in the camp, did non-Serb detainees continue to suffer beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time feel safe when you were in the camp in Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1149
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May we go into private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-1149, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal. You are free to go, but just wait a moment while the blinds are lowered. And we will begin the next session with the next witness in court. Yes. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Sabine Bauer for the Prosecution. Examined by Ms. Bauer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Marko Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, did you have the occasion on 19 June 2003 to review your witness statement in the presence of a court officer?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I didn't have time to review that statement because that was when the shelling of Zadar started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry. You misunderstand me. Did you, a month ago in Zadar, have an opportunity to review your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And signed a declaration attesting to its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. A month or two ago, I don't remember, I did sign a statement. I read it in front of a representative of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, pursuant to a court order on the 11th of April, 2003, the portions relating to paragraphs 13 and 14 and paragraphs 25 and 26 of the statement will be heard viva voce. However, I commence with the summary first. The witness is a Croat by ethnicity and was 40 years of age at the time of the events. Until May 1991, he was a JNA marine officer. Subsequently, he worked for the Croatian police in Zadar as a mine and explosive expert in charge of deactivating mines. In September 1991, the witness was sent by the Zadar MUP and Crisis Committee to organise the civilian protection in and around Skabrnja. For Your Honours' orientation, you will find Zadar and Skabrnja in the Croatian atlas at pages 24 and 25, grid references 2-C going over to 2-D. Skabrnja was inhabited by around 2.000 Croats. The village had neither military facilities nor any defence structures. Upon arrival in Skabrnja, the witness divided the 240 male villagers of Skabrnja into squads. The villagers of Skabrnja did not have any heavy weaponry nor were there any JNA officers located there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I apologise. The witness instructed the villagers to build trenches and erect barricades. However, traffic was not interrupted or blocked. The witness concluded, based on his military experience, that around 3.000 soldiers with good military training and equipment were required to successfully defend the village against an attack. At the end of September, the village of Skabrnja was shelled for the first time by the JNA. They used incendiary bombs and set the surrounding forest on fire. When people attempted to extinguish these fires, they were shot at. On 1st October the witness evacuated the civilian population from Skabrnja. Around 245 men, including medical personnel, stayed behind. The following day, the JNA attacked Nadin and Zemunik Gornji using infantry and tanks. When people from Nadin fled through Skabrnja, the air force attacked Skabrnja using cluster and incendiary bombs, killing two people in Nadin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, in October of 1991, did your men capture two JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: That is true. They captured two JNA officers who had come to the village in the afternoon, and they were Dejan Brener and Captain Jovanovic. I do not recall his first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of them before that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I didn't know them. I'd never seen them before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Officer Brener, did he introduce himself to you by his name?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Officer Brener gave an entirely different first and last name that day. He introduced himself as Esad Catic from Bihac. He said that he was chief of the military restaurant in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you for the first time learn the real identity of Officer Brener?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Five days later, I learnt from the police that he was not Esad Catic but a JNA Lieutenant Dejan Brener. And Jovanovic was a captain. As I say, I don't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you have a conversation with the person that gave you a wrong name?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a conversation of about two hours, and he gave me these data that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat for the Court's attention, what exactly did this person tell you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brener told me then, "I am surprised. Why are you working there? What are you waiting for? Mladic will certainly attack you. He will burn you down and destroy you, because simply you don't stand a chance." And then I said to him, "What do you mean?" And he said, "I know that for certain, because he will not allow you to stay there, because just look around: Above you in the neighbouring villages you have Serb populated areas." There were tanks, troops, and so on. I told him not to worry, that no one would attack us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Ratko Mladic at that time personally?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because before joining the Croatian police, I was a JNA member, and my command was in Knin, so that I did know Ratko Mladic by sight. I knew his voice. I never had any personal communication with him because he was a very high-ranking officer and I was not and there was a very explicit hierarchy in the former JNA so that I never had a chance to talk to him actually in person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times would you estimate you have seen Ratko Mladic at the time before you retired from the JNA service?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Maybe five, five to seven times perhaps, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come across Officer Brener later again?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I did. As I said, I met him again in the police in Zadar, and I heard then that his name was not Esad Catic but Dejan Brener, that he was an intelligence officer of the 9th Knin Corps, and I saw him wearing the uniform of the National Guards Corps, and he addressed me with the words, "You see, Marko, I too now am a member of the ZNGs."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear or learn later what happened to Officer Brener?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I know that he trained members of the ZNG in manning tanks, because the ZNGs had two tanks then that were part of the newly formed 112th Brigade, and Mr. Brener trained them. And then I heard in the police that Ratko Mladic had a very keen interest in him and that he was demanding that he be returned, so that later on there were negotiations in the Kolovare Hotel over Brener's return. He brought his mother, and Brener's wife and children were under Ratko Mladic's control, so that after a month or a month and a half, he was exchanged and he went back to Knin. As for his fate after that, I don't know. I never heard of him nor do I know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I'll continue with the summary. In November 1991, the inhabitants of Skabrnja returned to the village after a cease-fire agreement. The witness was under strict instructions from the Zadar crisis committee to uphold the cease-fire and not to respond to any provocations. Life in Skabrnja returned to normal. No JNA attacks occurred until the 18th of November. The JNA neither negotiated nor posed an ultimatum. They moved freely in the area including through the village of Skabrnja. On 18th November, 1991, the JNA attacked the village by shelling in the early morning hours. Civilians were directed to hide in their basements. The witness estimated, based on his military experience and information, that the village was attacked by at least 1.000 soldiers. There were 28 tanks coming from different directions followed by JNA trucks full of infantry soldiers. The witness went to his headquarters which was set up in a civilian house where he had a radio communications link with the Zadar Crisis Committee. Around midday of 18th November, the witness heard a loud explosion and observed from the highest point of Skabrnja a cloud of smoke. He concluded that a JNA truck with ammunition had exploded. After the explosion, the witness returned to the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, on that occasion did you have an opportunity to overhear a JNA radio communication on the network?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Throughout the day I listened to communications because it was an open line. It's an ordinary police radio station that worked on batteries - we didn't have electricity in the village - and I was simply listening to various interceptions and conversations and so I heard a conversation, among others, between then-Colonel Ratko Mladic and Lieutenant Colonel Tripko Cecovic who was commander of the 62nd Motorised Brigade from Benkovac, and I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they address each other?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: It was not coded. They spoke openly. And at the request of Mr. Tripko Cecovic, who said that his ammunition reserves had exploded and that he couldn't go on, Mr. Ratko Mladic said - I knew his voice, as I was saying - ordered him quite openly, using his name. He said,"Cecovic, continue the attack. You will get ammunition reserves. If you retreat, I will execute it -- you." Those were the words he used. In the basement there were another 60 civilians with me, women and old men, and they heard that conversation. It was nothing that couldn't be heard. It was heard loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Cecovic, did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was in Benkovac. And as I worked closely with the engineers, building, construction, et cetera, I often went to Benkovac to work on the maintenance of buildings, so that I would come across Tripko Cecovic very frequently in Benkovac. That is, before I left the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I'll continue with the summary: After the conversation with Ratko Mladic, the witness observed through his binoculars several helicopters landing in the surrounding areas of Skabrnja. Some JNA soldiers were unloading goods but due to distance, the witness couldn't tell what exactly. Further, he saw young soldiers dressed in dark uniforms getting out of some of the helicopters and taking up combat positions around the village of Skabrnja. The witness took them for JNA special forces based on their appearance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, what kind of special forces did you think they were at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I didn't actually see their faces, whether they were young or older people, but I could only judge by their uniforms. They wore dark blue uniforms and berets, and they were getting out of helicopters. Three or four helicopters landed two or three times, and soldiers got off. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In my judgement, as I was more or less familiar with the structure of the former JNA, in my personal opinion, I think they were special forces or elite units judging by their uniform, their appearance, and their subsequent activities. I think they were special units, probably -- probably a special unit, maybe a parachute unit from Nis or something like that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I'll continue with the summary: The attack resumed and Skabrnja was soon divided in two parts. The JNA tanks and infantry soldiers in SMB, dark blue, or camouflage uniforms took the western part of the village. The witness was informed by some of the villagers that JNA soldiers dragged civilians out of the basements, killed some of them on the spot and used others, including women and children, as human shields. The witness could recognise several people taken as human shields through his binoculars. In the late afternoon there was another air attack and the witness lost all his means of communication. During the evening and night, all civilians from the unoccupied part of the village fled to Zadar. The witness withdrew with his men in the early morning hours of the next day. The witness lists in his statement 42 villagers of Skabrnja who lost their lives during the attack. He also reviewed photographs of dead persons, some of which are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please read slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Apologies. He also reviewed photographs of dead persons, some of which are attached to his statement. Upon returning to Skabrnja in 1995, the witness saw about 80 per cent of the 500 Croat houses were totally destroyed. The witness observed that there were some destruction before and during the shelling attack on Skabrnja, but most of the houses were still inhabitable until the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Miljanic, you mentioned that before. Did you give a statement to a Croatian investigative Judge in 1992 about the events in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a bit hard of hearing, so at first I thought of that statement. This was in 1992, in the autumn of 1992. I gave a statement to Mr. Mikolcevic, investigating judge. He invited me to give a statement in relation to this massacre, this crime in Skabrnja. So that's the way it was. And I did that. I did that in his presence and in the presence of his secretary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, please just yes or no to the next two questions. Did you have an opportunity over the weekend to go over this statement?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to explain, if asked by the Judges or Mr. Milosevic, what if everything -- what the reasons were why the statement might appear on some occasions different from the ICTY statement?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: You have to know that a lot of time has gone by. Many things happened after that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, I just ask you to say yes or no, whether you are able to give the reasons for the differences.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I can. Well, yes, I gave that statement approximately over, say, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: No further questions. Your Honour, we have the statement for distribution, if need arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be as well if we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the end of May 1991, you were a JNA officer or, rather, a first class warrant officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the moment when you left the JNA, you were in Zadar within the Marine Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you left because you did not want to fight against your own people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, though, that as a former officer of the JNA, I assume that you knew that already from the month of May 1991, JNA barracks in Zadar - and not only in Zadar but also in Split and Sinj and Sibenik - were blockaded by the Croatian army, the ZNG, the MUP and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: That's not right, because quite simply how could they otherwise get food, water, electricity, and everything else? Nobody impeded them in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were not under blockade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The barracks in Split, Zadar, Sinj and Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Zadar. I'm talking about Zadar. I know about Zadar, I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that barracks were not under blockade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the blockade start, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, when the first shells started falling on Zadar. This was sometime in August, the month of August. That's when the blockade of the barracks started. But soldiers were leaving the barracks en masse, and these same barracks were receiving food, that is to say, from town, because in Zadar, there was not a military bakery. So food, electricity, water, medical assistance, that's what all the barracks got.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, when did this stop, what you refer to, food, electricity, water, and when was gunfire opened at barracks and garrisons of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: When the Serb paramilitary units cut off the electricity supply and the water supply of the town of Zadar and everything else. That's when it started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: This started sometime in August. I think it was the month of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, since you should certainly know about that, that General Spegelj, in his order issued as far as back as the 5th of December, 1990, he ordered complete surveillance of all JNA activity in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that because at that time I was still a member of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the Defence Ministry of Croatia sending a telegram to the MUPs in 17 Croatian municipalities, and this telegram said, "Be prepared and ready to operate vis-a-vis barracks and garrisons according to assignments issued"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I never saw this order nor did I ever receive it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And later, as an officer of the JNA, did you know or as an officer of the Guards Corps did you know that only in the year 1991 there were 268 attacks at JNA officers throughout Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: First of all, I was not an officer of the National Guards Corps, because had I been an officer of the ZNG, I would have had at least the rank I had in the JNA. I am a man who does not even have the rank of corporal in the Croatian army. I was a member of the regular force of the MUP, and I dealt with mines and explosives since I -- this was my line of work and that's why I worked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you know as a member of the regular MUP forces that only in 1991 there were 268 attacks at JNA officers throughout Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that 100 -- that there were 107 cases of JNA officers being brought into custody, arrested at the MUP and that they had their weapons taken away from them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I repeat once again, I did not have a high-ranking position. I was an ordinary policeman, and later on I became an inspector. So I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of many cases when JNA officers' apartments were broken into and when they were looted, when their valuables were taken and their families attacked?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know, because I myself live in that kind of neighbourhood in Zadar where there were only military apartments. Only military apartments. And as for these officers with whom I worked and with whom I lived, I invariably had good, correct relations with them. And all the people -- all these people left when the JNA was moving out of the town of Zadar. Until the very last moment, I lived with them together in the same apartment building, right next door. Major Obradovic, a JNA pilot, lived right next to me, in the apartment right next to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for such an extensive answer. And do you know who was the Chief of Staff of the Marine Corps in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Lieutenant Colonel Srecko Lakic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, because he and I served together in Losinj. In addition to that, he comes from the area that I come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that his wife, who was a Croat, was killed in front of the barracks in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: It's not true. She was not killed. His children still live in Losinj and their mother, his wife, died. And the doctor offered Mr. Lakic to go to see his wife, and she was seriously ill psychologically. Mrs. Milena Lakic. And it's not true. Nobody killed her. Mr. Togilja [phoen] from the Crisis Staff went, together with the doctor, and the doctor was supposed to stay by way of a guarantee at the barracks in Sibenik, and he was going to see his wife with the doctor and with Mr. Togilja, and his two children, the two children. Mr. Srecko Lakic went along too and they asked him, "Father, go and see Mother." That is the truth, Mr. Milosevic. She was not killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the families were brought in front of the barracks, brought by the representatives of the Croat authorities and that they asked Lieutenant Colonel Lakic to hand over the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You're saying no, so we can go on.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Soon after you left the JNA you were sent to Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No. No. I spent four months or perhaps even more than that in Zadar before I went to Skabrnja, because Skabrnja is my native village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after four months you went to Skabrnja to organise the civilian defence there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. And not to allow my provocations, in accordance with the orders of the chief of police, Mr. Brzoje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before that, before you went to Skabrnja, was there a blockade of the barracks in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, no. There was no blockade of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, were there any attacks at Skabrnja before September 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Forests were torched and livestock was taken away. The harvest was destroyed. Every day there were fires. There was arson. All sorts of terrible things were done around that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who took away the cattle and burned the harvest and forests?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Who? I don't know. I really cannot answer that, because I really don't know. I didn't see anyone myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the units of the JNA, did they want to have the barracks in Zadar, Sibenik, Split, and Sinj blocked?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as for Sibenik, Sinj, Split, I really don't know about that. As for Zadar is concerned, they did not opt for a deblockade. I know that quite simply because many soldiers, among who I was -- or, rather, I was their commander, they were fleeing from the barracks and they came to us. They came to me. They came to their former superior officers, and they came with weapons and they threw their weapons away and said that they were leaving. And also they took them in to the police and civilian defence, wherever, and then they gave them clothing and then they left. About 150 or 200 soldiers would sometimes leave the barracks in one day only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you something else. Was this the route that was taken through Skabrnja through which these forces were supposed to get close to the barracks in Sibenik, Split, and Sinj from the Split Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, no. There were special communication from Sinj to Sibenik -- I mean from Knin to Sibenik, and there is special communication for Sibenik and Split and Zadar is independent, because Benkovac is between Zadar and Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was not necessary to go via this route in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No. No. There's this other road from Smiljetici [phoen] going via Zemunik, Smokovici to the airport, and then to Zadar ultimately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was one of the routes, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was one of the routes. And this communication was open throughout this time. Well, throughout this time, because Mr. Mladic precisely took this route when he went to negotiation in Zadar. That is to say that this had to do with Mr. Brener and the hotel Kolovare. I saw him myself as he passed by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that on the 15th of August, 1991, the General Staff of the JNA issued an order to deblock all JNA barracks in territories that were not in jeopardy?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is correct that Skabrnja was one of these points when the JNA moved towards Zadar and Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but inside there weren't any --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's the only thing I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time, and bear in mind the interpreters. Would you do the same, please, Mr. Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this room, a transcript appeared of an intercept of a telephone conversation between General Veljko Kadijevic and Croatian President Tudjman. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard this, that Kadijevic asked Tudjman to stop attacks in barracks in Sibenik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The witness doesn't know anything about this. He said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In relation to these blockades of barracks, do you know that even the bodies of killed JNA soldiers and officers could not be buried, that they were put away and they were buried only later because barracks were under pressure, under blockade?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know about any of this, let's move on to those things that you must be aware of. You say that in Skabrnja you organised a civilian defence. Two hundred forty locals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Separated into two groups.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: As for weapons, we had -- about 40 per cent were hunting weapons, sports weapons, and trophies from the Second World War. Also, about 10 per cent of military weapons. That is to say, semi-automatic and automatic rifles. As for heavy infantry weapons, two hand-held launchers with four mines respectively, and two 82-millimetre launchers that were in Karlovac. So they had about 20 mines each. That's the weapons we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was everything that you had at that particular point on the route leading to Zadar and Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, not directly at that particular point because this was about 7 kilometres away. It was about 7 kilometres away, because Skabrnja is about eight and a half kilometres. Yes, it's about 7 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So it was scattered throughout this area.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Towards Zadar and Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it correct that in addition to the locals that you've been referring to organised in the so-called Skabrnja Battalion, there were also 600 members of the ZNG from Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, that's not true, because first of all, it was not a battalion. I mean, it was a battalion, but the word "Bojna" was not used. At that time, we were using the terminology that was used in the former JNA. So the word used was "battalion." We didn't use the word "Bojna" yet. And in the -- as for the ZNG, no one was ever in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You know who Rudolf Davorin is, you've heard of that name, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Rudolf Davorin from Zagreb. Well, he was -- I don't know, he was deputy Prime Minister or something. Or an ambassador some kind of ambassador.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 22nd of September, 1991, on behalf of the Croatia, in Zipnic [phoen], he signed an agreement that had to do with the deblockade of JNA barracks and garrisons? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that because I did not hold that kind of position. I could not know about such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But as you come from Zadar yourself, after this agreement was signed, were the barracks in Zadar under a blockade and shot at by the ZNG and MUP?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I have already told you this. I said that I arrived in Skabrnja and was there the whole time, and from time to time I would go down to Zadar to take what I needed; ammunition, bandages, and things of that sort. I went to ask them to give us those supplies. That was my assignment and task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well, Mr. Miljanic. Let me just remind you of this: As the main points in the agreement were to stop the blockade of the barracks; second, to allow medical assistance to the wounded JNA members; third, to deal with all the consequences of the blockade; and fourth, to pull out the units peacefully --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no point asking him this. He knows nothing about the agreement. He was in Skabrnja. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he would go to Zadar, and that's close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was in command of the garrison of the JNA in Zadar at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, I think it was Mr. -- He was a colonel, at any rate. Momcilo Perisic. I think it was Momcilo Perisic. He was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you happen to recall that during those attacks 11 soldiers belonging to the JNA were killed within the frameworks of that barracks in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, to go back to Skabrnja for a moment, in paragraph 8 of your statement you claim that before the attack there was no shooting from your side or any sort of provocations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me this: Why, then, did the JNA members open fire?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really can't say why they went into action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that it was from the forests around Skabrnja that fire was opened targeting the JNA units?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, never. And I can say that with full responsibility. There was never any shooting, because quite simply we didn't dare provoke them because we didn't have the force to back us up to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know that Skabrnja was what you in the army call a collection point where the JNA was supposed to collect and this was a target from the surrounding forests, as a standby?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: It wasn't -- Skabrnja was never an important strategic point. Even when I was a member of the JNA, it wasn't a strategic area of any kind. It was just referred to as cleric and nationalist and an Ustasha village, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to enter into qualifications of that kind, but a moment ago we ascertained it was a point on the road towards Zadar and Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was a main road going past there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm talking about. It was a main road passing that way. Now you stand by what you said, that you had 240 fighters in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you had nobody else, no other ZNG members from Zadar or anybody else except those 240 fighters of yours, combatants.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Skabrnja when I say that. Now, the other villages remain, the seven largest villages in the Zadar municipality, because the territory which I controlled as a policeman made up a third of the Zadar municipality. So within that composition, within that third, there were seven large villages. So in Skabrnja there were 250 men, and up to the 700-odd people in all the other villages around Zadar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: Now, what is the radius of that area, the diameter? You say that there were 240 of you in Skabrnja and 800 in the other villages.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: 240, as I said, and then another 400 and something in the other villages around, and the diameter, I would say, was about 30-odd kilometres. Usually for the most part it was an imaginary line, and that covered about 38 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that within those efforts for the units to break through to the Zadar road, that Zoran Stevanovic from Brdsa [phoen], a lieutenant, was killed and that another ten were seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Where did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that area, the area of the JNA units when their barracks were under blockade tried to break through?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe on that day when there was fighting, but not before that. Nobody ever got killed in Skabrnja before that except for three locals who died from a shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know of the death of Lieutenant Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let's not waste time. He's said that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the JNA units manage to break through towards Zemunik and Borik immediately after that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: What time do you have in mind, what period of time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Immediately after those conflicts and clashes on the Skabrnja axis.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know where the JNA went to after that. I just know that before Skabrnja fell, the JNA units were in Crno at the crossing towards the town of Zadar. As for the rest, I don't know. They didn't need to break through anywhere because they were already at Smokovici and Zemunik, so where would they have to break through, which territory?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this then: Is it true that the first combat operations took part in Skabrnja itself?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, where did the fighting take place first?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: In Kijevo, Krusevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Polaca, Kijevo, Krusevo; lots of other place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know that during that period of time the person in command was Vlado Vukovic who at the time was the commander of the 9th Knin Corps, and not General Mladic? General Mladic was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: He was a colonel. Mladic wasn't a general at the time and Vukovic did arrive for negotiations in Zadar before Mladic, and so did Hasovic. Hasovic came in for negotiations too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vukovic was commander of the 9th Corps and Mladic was Chief of Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he was Colonel Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say this and repeat it in paragraph 15 of your report, that three locals of Skabrnja lost their lives during the shelling of Skabrnja by the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Before the 18th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But in paragraph 10 you said that on the 1st of October, 1991, you organised the evacuation of women, children, and elderly persons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that what was left in Skabrnja were the combatants.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, just the men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just the combatants, the fighters under your command; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, it was something between combatants and Civil Defence because people of 55 or 60, men of 55 or 60 can't really be called combatants, but if you like to call them that, then all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the civilian population was evacuated before the conflict, and in Skabrnja during the conflict the only people who stayed on were the military men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can put it that way if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. So these three locals were in fact combatants who were killed in the fighting against members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't combatants. No. The shells hit them and two of them died of mortar shells, one from a cannon shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's put that the people left in the village after the evacuation were combatants. That's the word that the accused continually uses. Now, you should have the opportunity to answer that and clarify, if you would, who it was who left. Would you describe them as combatants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, they were members of the Civil Defence forces, that is to say Civil Defence. Now, how we're going to treat them now and refer to them, I simply don't know. What they were was members of the Civil Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the witness has already given that answer and specified that there were 240 of them and that it was a unit which went into operation in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was anybody else left besides the members of the Civil Defence? Were there any other men at all or were they all members of that Civil Defence and the unit as the accused describes it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
