utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't actually a unit of any kind. And I said at the beginning that we created the structure on the basis of the Civil Defence that existed in the former Yugoslavia, and Civil Defence had the task of preventing fires, elemental disasters, wars, to defend the population, find shelter if there was a natural disaster. So that was the task and aim of what -- what we're now calling and referring to as a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that unit was armed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Partially armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all the civilians before that, as it says here in paragraph 10 of your statement, on the 1st of October, were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, let's look at paragraph 17, where you say that the JNA passed through the village every day, that you did not provoke them because those were the orders you received. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Quite true, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also, however, true that your fighters opened fire almost every day at the members of the JNA and that in that firing six JNA members were killed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: That's not true. Not a single soldier was killed by my people in the Civil Defence, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that your people, the people under your command, didn't kill anybody?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, they did not kill anybody up until the 18th, and that was during the fighting, and I allow for that possibility, that during the fighting that might have happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 19 you say on the 18th of November that around 0725 hours in the morning an attack on Skabrnja started and at the beginning there were only two women. However, in paragraph 22, you go on to say that the first civilians were killed at around 1130 hours.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what about these women, were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were civilians, elderly women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how come, when you said you evacuated everybody before that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that on the 5th, The Hague truce was signed and I was given orders to return all civilians back to the village. And then Skabrnja was attacked during this truce, during the cease-fire, Mr. Milosevic. And I was given orders from the chief of police and from the Crisis Staff that an agreement had been signed in The Hague about a cease-fire and that everybody should go back to Skabrnja. And they were indeed returned from the island of Ugljan, and they were boarded up onto buses, five buses, and they all returned to Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now tell me this then, please. Let's clarify one point: How do you know when these two women were killed? Did you see them being killed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was informed by a nurse, and her name was Danka Drazen. She was in the cellar together with doctor Boris Celalija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were they killed, by shells?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, by shells, both of them. One of them died in the hospital at Zadar whereas Mrs. Brkic died on the spot. She was killed on the spot. And Zilic, the other woman, died in the Zadar hospital and both her legs were blown away by the shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was before the attack, was it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No. It was during the attack, at about 11:00 or 12.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that it began at 7.25.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, the attack on Skabrnja began at 7.25 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the first casualties were at around 11.30, were they?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, those were the first casualties. Whether anybody was killed before that, I don't know. Nobody informed me nor did I know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: In paragraph 22, you say that your father, as well as Krsta Segaric, Stana Vickovic, and Luka Segaric --

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Luca is his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Luca, I see. She's a woman.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, she's a woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Luca Segaric, she was pulled out of the basement by JNA soldiers and then these people were all killed.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, because my mother was an eyewitness when they killed my father. That's why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I understood it that a boy by the name of Segaric, who was 13 years old, told you about it.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, he told me first but my mother told me about it afterwards. I never plucked up the courage to ask her myself. But she told me how it was, how he was tied with some wire, he had to lean down, she was in another cellar and they took her to the detention centre in Benkovac but they killed him on the spot, him and the others, the rest of them. That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is that what you describe in your statement, the one you gave in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I described it that way in my statement. I can't remember any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Bauer asked you whether you could explain the difference between what you said in your statement then and the statement given to the investigators. So I'd like to ask you to explain that to me now, please.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Let me explain, yes. I gave the statement under some very strange circumstances. When we started the statement, the Judge Vlado Mikolcevic and his secretary and myself, after an hour or a little more -- actually, the town of Zadar was shelled, and the secretary, Vlado Mikolcevic's secretary, the lady said, "I can't stay here any longer. We're going to get killed. I have to leave." And Vlado said, "Marko, we have nothing more to do here. Just sign your statement and we've finished our interview," and that's how it was. Now, when this second statement was given, I had two days at my disposal, two days' time, two hours a day, or two or three hours per day, so I had time to talk to the people and remember how everything happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. With the explanation that you've given, I don't want to bother you with the differences. Shells were falling all over the place, and in fact you weren't able to finish and conclude your interview. But when you gave your second statement, there were no shells.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: It was peacetime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. All right. Mr. Miljanic, I accept that explanation that you've just given us, but tell me this, please, Mr. Miljanic, as this relates to your -- paragraph 22 of your statement, where you say how these people were killed, including your father, that they pulled them out of the basement, are you quite sure that they were JNA soldiers or perhaps it was a paramilitary formation that was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer to that question. I didn't see it with my own eyes. Quite simply, I don't know who the perpetrators were. But according to what my mother told me and all the others who were there, they say that they were all wearing masks and they had black paint on their faces. So I really can't say. I don't know whether they were JNA soldiers or paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, all right. As you yourself were a JNA officer, does it seem to you to be logical that it was the -- that JNA soldiers should have been masked and painted, had -- with black paint on their faces like that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, when you went into operation, you would do all sorts of things, and we know of an attack that when an attack takes place on a town or a village you assess the tactical situation, you make an evaluation, you size the up the situation, and then you issue orders for an assignment. Now, what they decided to do, how they decided to go into action, I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, if -- Mr. Miljanic, this is a very important point. You can't say for certain who those people were.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let's try and do this indirectly. Is it true, in a round Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about way, Mr. Miljanic, at the point that these killings happened the JNA units had already passed through Skabrnja and continued along the road to Zadar for the deblockade? Isn't that right? Hadn't the JNA just passed through? This happened once they had already passed through; right? They had already gone.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No. The units there were together, the JNA units. Actually, the composition was mixed, and there were no problems with respect to the deblockade, because the Serbs, our neighbours, could pass through Skabrnja quite freely to the last, very last day. So I don't know why they would have to do away with some blockades. There were two checkpoints in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not talking about the blockade. I'm talking about the blockade that was to come. What I want to say is that they passed through Skabrnja and when the killings took place, according to my information, the JNA units had already passed through Skabrnja and left and that the killings were perpetrated by some members of paramilitary formations from the region, not JNA soldiers. That's what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you one way or another. I can't say who did the killing you. I don't know. Because I didn't see it with my very own eyes. Had I seen who had done it, I wouldn't be here today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Miljanic. As I can see from paragraph 24 of your statement, when these killings took place, that is to say around 11.30, you were up on a hill called Razovljeva Glavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes -- No. Actually, no. I was on the hill, Razovljeva Glavica hill in the morning when the attack started, in actual fact. And then I went down into the village when the attack started and was in the basement of Tonko Skara's house, where the radio station was in that basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where were you at 11.30 when the killing took place?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I was in the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At 11.30 you mean?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, at 11.30 I was in the basement of the Mr. Skara's house, Mr. Skara's basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you hear that terrible explosion when the truck blew up, the JNA truck that you described during your live testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: That was around 12.00. Between 11:00 and 12.00. I can't remember exactly. I went outside, and now as that part of village is slightly raised, it's on a small hill, I went up front and heard this resounding explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me where the truck was exactly. Had it already passed through Skabrnja or was it in front of Skabrnja? Had it already passed Skabrnja or was it at the entrance to Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: The Benkovac-Zadar road goes from one end of Skabrnja to the other, so it was somewhere towards Gornji Zemunik, in that area, and most probably our forces weren't there. There were none of our men there, because at that time, the explosion took place between 11:00 and 12.00, I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the truck had already passed Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, it was still in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was still in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that it could have been destroyed by a hand grenade thrown by one of your combatants?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, there is that possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after that you said you went back to your office in order to maintain radio links with Zadar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Miljanic, according to your statement, there was an all-out attack going on on Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say that around 1.000 soldiers attacked the village, that the civilians were killed, and you yourself at your command post where you had these links, radio links with Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: In the basement. It's got nothing to do with the command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But all the time you were in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, along with 65 civilians. Between 60 and 70 civilians, in actual fact. We were in the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that over the radio you heard a conversation between Mladic and Cecovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that came after the explosion, after 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Around 12.00. Just after that. Perhaps, as far as I can remember, it might have been some 15 minutes to half an hour after the explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So after 12.00. Does that mean that the conversation took place after the JNA forces had passed Skabrnja and left it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, because during that first day, the JNA reached the centre of the village and there was the other half of the village that wasn't occupied that day by 8.00 at night. So they had taken control of half the village but other half remained. They had parked their tanks and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did Mladic insist upon them going on further towards Zadar and Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't going towards Zadar. It's the other way, the opposite direction. They were going towards Nadin, because Nadin was closer to Benkovac. Nadin, that's where they were going, Nadin and Benkovac, that's the direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the situation like in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't in Benkovac since June or July 1991. I haven't been to Benkovac since then. We didn't dare pass by that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. From what you're saying as they were -- the -- they were conversing and they referred to each other by their surnames, and Mladic insisted upon going forward, further on.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was your official radio station, the usual kind that the police station had?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. And we had a generator. We had a car battery, otherwise there was no electricity because the paramilitaries cut off electricity and all other supplies to Skabrnja. There was nothing, so that's what we had to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's past the time for the adjournment so we'll adjourn now. Mr. Miljanic, could I ask you to remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, tell me, please, what kind of radio station did you have on you when you overheard this conversation, and on which frequency?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I had a police radio station from a police vehicle that I had brought from the police administration. It is an ordinary police radio station, and Motorolas, but I didn't have a single Motorola. So it was an open frequency. I think it was 64 -- I was 64, and I had a direct connection with the information centre in Zadar. Yes, a direct line with the information centre in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the same frequency that you had a connection with the information line was being used by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Everything could be heard every day, not just that day. There were interceptions. It was possible. It was not a protected, encrypted line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, since you caught that conversation, did you have occasion to hear any other conversation that Mladic may have had with other officers?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard any other conversation, only that one. I heard from other -- I heard talks by other JNA members, Petar Radmanovic, and others who called me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, since you served in the marines, can you tell us in a couple of words what the uniform of the marines looked like, in two words.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: It was a regular SMB uniform and a beret. The beret was black, and there were two rifles and an anchor. I can't remember whether it was the right or left sleeve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the marines did not wear blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: While I was there, no, because I have to tell you that as I was later on a commander of the construction company in Zadar, and at Losinj, together with Lakic, I was in the marine assault infantry. So it didn't have blue uniforms at the time, no, only SMB uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did it have blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was after I left the marines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you mentioned the Parachute Brigade from Nis, do you know that it couldn't have had blue uniforms? You say that people were coming out of helicopters wearing blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that they did have an SMB uniform before, but during the changes that occurred, I don't know, but I assume, because the helicopters, three at a time, landed three or four times, and infantry came out of them. So I don't know. I am not claiming explicitly that they were special forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, that's sufficient. In paragraph 27, you say that JNA soldiers, those that came out of helicopter, surrounded you and formed some kind of combat formation. How did you manage to get away?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I had a corridor - I don't have a map here - that led towards a place called Prkos, a narrow corridor. And that night I managed to pull out all the surviving civilians along that corridor, as well as all the members of the Civil Defence. The entire personnel that night were pulled out of that part of the village via Vlacine, a former Italian airport during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 28, you say that the JNA in 16.30 managed to divide Skabrnja into two parts. No, at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say after all that fighting, 1.000 troops, helicopters, special forces, a great deal of weapons, the JNA did not manage to overcome the resistance of 240 locals, as you say, who were 40 per cent armed with hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. They reached halfway into the village. The tank climbed to the so-called Razovljeva Glavica, and then all operations ceased. I don't know why that happened but it happened. Perhaps maybe somebody ordered a cease-fire, because you say that that was a time of truce.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the truce was before, when I brought the civilians back to Skabrnja. That is when the truce was signed. That is what I was told by the head of the police administration in writing. He gave me that order, "A truce has been signed in The Hague, so bring back the civilians."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in 29 that your connection with Zadar was interrupted after an air attack.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened before it was cut off?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: The aerial was on an oak, it was about six metres high, and a plane came, shelled and cut off this tree and the aerial fell down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 32, you say that you personally left at 5.30 the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. And during the night, I went to seek assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that fighting went on continuously for 22 hours?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No. During the night there was no resistance, no shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true, Mr. Miljanic, that Skabrnja would not have been attacked at all if you were not supposed, following orders from Zadar, to prevent the Knin Corps from reaching Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, JNA units were behind our backs. Skabrnja is 18 kilometres from Zadar and Crno and Smokovici were five kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. I understand the explanation. And is it true that you didn't see a single killing of any civilian from Skabrnja committed allegedly by any JNA member?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any killing. I only saw photographs and heard stories afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, and in paragraph 34 you yourself say that many civilians were killed during the attack and after it. Who could have killed those civilians after the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but a group of civilians were killed two months later in February 1992, the people that had stayed behind in Skabrnja. I don't know who killed them. I can't say when I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true, Mr. Miljanic, that you as a witness in connection with events in Skabrnja have already appeared before the District Court in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that those proceedings in which you testified were renewed? The number was K2594, then it acquired a new number, K6701.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know that. When I'm called or when I'm summoned -- the last trial I was summoned to was Mrs. Zorana Banic. She was on trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, who are the accused in those proceedings? Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you also testified about these events in the trial of Zorana Banic also before the Croatian court in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just said that I did testify in those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are those proceedings being conducted under the supervision of this opposite side here that you were examined by just now?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Under their supervision, yes. There are gentlemen, I don't know them, but probably they come from this institution. I don't know who they belong to. They were always there whenever I testified in Zadar. I don't know whether they were there on other days.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume, Mr. May, that there are statements of witnesses from those trials as they are being conducted under the supervision of the side opposite. So I would just like to object to the fact that I have not been served with those statements, and in view of this testimony, I should have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you, Mr. Miljanic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before we go any further, if they are relevant for disclosure, they will be disclosed. It's a matter for the Prosecution, but they have a duty to disclose anything which may be exculpatory, anything, that is, which might help your defence. Now, you've got about five minutes left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best to complete my questions on the basis of the limited information that my associates were able to collect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have here Neue Zuricher Zeitung of December 22nd, 2001. Since you haven't seen that, I won't bother you with the document itself, but as you're testifying in that case, my question is do you know whether the following is true as it has to do with Mrs. Banic, who is an accused in those proceedings. And it says in a paragraph: "Read statement of eyewitnesses to the massacre appeared in the Croatian media claiming [In English] to have seen the nurse participating in the killing. Croatian human rights circles say the woman is real guilty. She's presently being held in the Zadar prison where she has, among other things, the right to visits from International Red Cross delegates. In the Banic case, it may be expected that the same eyewitnesses will testify in a new trial. They claim to have seen the nurse stabbing an elderly man with a knife and then participating in the running armoured vehicle over the fresh corpses."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, what has this to do with the witness? Is there any reference to him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just finish this last sentence? [In English] "took part in the massacres." [Interpretation] Strbac who was also there, all armed and in camouflage uniforms."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you know, Mr. Miljanic, that it was absolutely not possible for any women to be in the JNA in those days wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This has absolutely nothing to do with the witness at all. Yes. Is there anything else you've got to ask him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the commander of the 9th Corps, General Vukovic, after those events, called Milan Babic, asking him to react to the killings committed by members of paramilitary units, local units and not the JNA under any circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. As I say, I hear this for the first time today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever hear of the participation of any women in the participation of killings?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I've already told you that I personally didn't see anything, but my mother and other women and men who were captured on that day and taken to Benkovac told me about those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did they tell you? Did they see some women committing murder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all second or third-hand, and what this other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. case has to do with this case is not at all clear. You haven't made it clear. You can ask him about something else, and you've got about two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has it got something to do with this in view of the fact that women are appearing in the role of killers, which shows clearly that they couldn't have been members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Did you see any -- yourself see any women involved at Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't see anyone, any of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, men or women. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miljanic. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miljanic, let me first ask you a few questions linked to the statement that you gave to the investigators on the 24th and 25th of July, I think in 1995. And then I would like to show you a few things in connection with those same facts as you described them in your statement of the 5th of October, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the accused has accepted the account which the witness has given as to why there are discrepancies between the two, and I'm not sure that, in that sort of position, that it's helpful to have you then cross-examining about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, after the cross-examination by Mr. Milosevic, as this statement was referred to, I'm quite sure that no one noticed this, and the things stated in this statement, you as the Trial Chamber should be aware of. For instance, in his statement he said that following his command -- under his command there were 800 persons, and things like that. So I think that that statement should be something you should look into, because they have substantive matters raised. He said in that statement, for instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll exhibit that statement, and we can have a look at it ourselves. We'll get a Defence number for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness explain to us, was it 240 men or 800 men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's explained. He's explained he didn't have enough time to go through it. But he can answer the question. He can answer the question specifically. Was it 200 or 800?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the very beginning, I said that in Skabrnja itself, there were 240, but in all the other villages around me over which I had competence as a policeman, I had a total of 750 men. So Skabrnja plus Prkos, Galovac, Gorica, Nadin, Donji and Gornji Zemunik. So one-third of Zadar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Also in your statement you explained clearly that you learned the first and last names of the persons who had killed your father. You even gave the name, and you said that you had to give some money to learn about it, and you said that they were locals.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: In those days, I received information which later proved to be incorrect and unfounded, and without any grounds I had accused a gentleman called Mr. Draca. My accusations were unfounded because I had listened to people who had misinformed me. Hearing my mother and the other locals, I came to the conclusion that I had accused the wrong person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You even say that your father was armed and had taken part in the defence of the town. My father was a huntsman, and he had a Bokerica hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he defended the town.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, he had a rifle. Now, whether I said that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that we had asserted the command line from Nadin to Gornji Zemunik that no one could pass because we had dug out trenches and bunkers under the ground and minefields with more than 1.000 anti-tank and anti-personnel mines, and that you were in command of the placing of those mines.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: That's a mistake. There were a hundred, because even the JNA didn't have a thousand in those days. I said that we simply did make dugouts and divided the men up so as to cover the areas from which stealing occurred of the harvest, livestock, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you will read through this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my last question would be that members of the National Guards Corps were not there at all.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Not in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that they were there before the 2nd of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the day that tank was hit that exploded, you said that you sent those who came with anti-tank weapons, you sent them to a place from which they could hit the place where the tank was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain, if I may. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Skabrnja there were never any National Guards Corps members. They arrived in Nadin before I came there. There were some from the 112th brigade, a platoon in Nadin and not in Skabrnja who, after that, withdrew and never came. As for rockets, yes. That day some people came with I don't know how many rockets, and I gave them the assignment to hit tanks and they said they couldn't, it was too close, but my opinion is that they were afraid and they ran away. They didn't fire a single rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have the rest in the statement so I won't fatigue you any further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it should be given a C number since the accused himself didn't put it in. Yes, Ms. Bauer. Re-examined by Ms. Bauer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, in response to a question by Mr. Milosevic, you mentioned that on the 18th your radio communication lines had some interference and that the JNA officer called Petar Radmanovic called you. What was that, approximately, and what, in very, very brief terms, did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: That's correct. This Petar Radmanovic worked with me, together with me in the former army. He was a warrant officer of the JNA, just like I was. And on that day, at a given point in time, he called me over the radio transmitter. And when I asked Zadar for help through the information centre, he answered with the following words: "There is no help for you. It's better for you to hang yourself. That's better, because we are going to hang you, skin you, and to fry your liver on a grill." Though those are the exact words that Mr. Radmanovic addressed to me, my former colleague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else threaten you via these radio communication links on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC
utterances.text: Well, various threats were heard, but quite simply I did not have time to listen to all of this, but yes, there were, yes, because I already mentioned that it was not a protected communication line, so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: That would conclude my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness is C-1168, and I assume when she comes in also Mr. McKeon will come in because he's the one to lead the witness. He's definitely waiting outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, how long do you anticipate you will be with this witness in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Less than ten minutes, Your Honour. Somewhere between five and ten minutes. Not very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll have to consider what's an appropriate time to adjourn, because we won't be able to conclude her evidence today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One administrative matter. Although this witness is not testifying with any protective measures, there is one section of the proofing summary, which is the last paragraph, paragraph 8 of the proofing summary, and we're going to ask if we could have that dealt with in private session because it discusses another protected witness and the exhibit that I want to ask her about may make reference to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. McKeon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, is your full name Barbara Nadj?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in recent days, did you have an opportunity to go over your witness statement in the presence of an officer of the court and attest to its accuracy subject to corrections which you noted, and then did you sign the documentation showing that you had attested this statement?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I offer the statement of Barbara Nadj into evidence under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll get a number for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the following summary of the witness's statement. I am going to jump ahead, though, to the end to cover a couple of matters that came up to proofing when it comes up in the statement. This witness, Your Honour, is a Hungarian woman who was 49 years old at the time of the events in question, and at the time she was a resident of the village of Brestovac in the Baranja region of Croatia. She is the wife of victim Steven Nadj. The witness's husband was first arrested on 4 December 1991. He was taken to the building of the community centre in Grabovac, and when he finally returned home the next day, he was badly bruised over his entire body. After that, her husband had to report twice a day. He told her that most of the time he reported to a JNA captain. Moving to paragraph 6 of the proofing summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, could you tell us what sort of work it was that your husband did for a living and where he worked.

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: He worked in Brestovac as a metalworker at the farm in Bilje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point was your husband told that he could no longer work at that farm in Bilje; and if so, when did this occur?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: This happened in 1991, in December, on the 4th. He was no longer at work. He didn't have the right to go there. Nobody dared come to see us, and we didn't -- and we were not supposed to have any contacts with anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Returning to the summary, Your Honour, paragraph 3. On the 4th of May, 1992, a white-coloured minivan pulled in front of the witness's house. Three men came into the courtyard. One older man was dressed in a camouflage uniform, and two younger men were dressed in civilian clothes. They were armed with what seemed to the witness to be full metal automatic rifles. These men took the witness's husband away. She heard her husband ask where they were taking him, and they said, "For the interrogation." The older man asked her husband if he had been beaten, and when the answer was positive, the Serb told him that he had nothing to fear and that nobody would beat him now. Moving, Your Honour, to paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, when your husband's body was actually found, did it show evidence that he had in fact been beaten?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes. His ribs had been broken, and it was obvious that his skull had been broken and that he had also sustained gunshot wounds. I'm supposed to speak louder, but I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't upset yourself, and don't worry about speaking loudly. We'll deal with this as rapidly as we can. Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: In the summary, Your Honour, paragraph 4. In the following days, the witness tried to find out what happened to her husband and went to several places, but nobody knew anything. Several days later, she was told that he had been in the Beli Manastir prison. This was in the basement of a building used by the militia of the SAO Krajina. Upon her arrival there, she was told by the policeman that her husband was not there. The body was only found six years later at the Catholic cemetery in Beli Manastir. The witness heard on the day following the abduction that four other people had been taken away that night, and their bodies were exhumed together with the body of her husband. Your Honour, moving to paragraph 7 of the proofing summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, did you learn from the Croatian authorities that your husband and the four people that were buried with him were actually buried somewhere else before the Catholic cemetery and then reburied in that cemetery; and if so, where were they buried first?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes. They were all together in one grave. They were thrown in in bags at Beli Manastir, at the Catholic cemetery. And then there was a post-mortem, and then they saw which body was which one. Kopacki Rit and Tikves were the localities where they were found. That's where they were found because they were only in a shallow grave, and then they picked them up from there and they took them to the Catholic cemetery in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if we could go into private session for the last paragraph, 8, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's for you to cross-examine. It may be that you can do so in order that this witness can finish this afternoon rather than having to come back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try, Mr. May. Obviously, the witness is under stress, and I do not wish to hurt her in any way. Just a few questions. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This does not reveal the identity that Mr. McKeon wishes to protect, but a short while ago, you were asked some questions in closed session with regard to some persons whose names I'm not going to mention. You explained that these people who you mentioned came to put questions to you in order to ascertain who it was who took your husband away. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These men who came to put these questions to you and to establish who it was that had taken your husband away were Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were representatives of the Krajina police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Nadj. That's what I wish to clarify first of all. So representatives of the Krajina police came in order to try to establish the facts, namely who had taken your husband away. Now, please tell me, Mrs. Nadj, in your statement you say that there were problems in Baranja and that they started sometime in July 1991.

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that then Serb women and children surreptitiously left their houses. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the reasons why women and children of Serb ethnicity left Baranja?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Unfortunately, they did not tell us why they were leaving Baranja and we knew that they were all armed and they knew why they were leaving Baranja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that it was precisely the month of August, 1991 in Baranja a series of killings occurred, killings of Serb -- persons of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 2nd of August of 1991, in Darda, Milivoje Stojakovic was killed in his own backyard?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: I just know what happened in Grabovac. I don't know about the other villages, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Baranja is not that big. Do you remember perhaps that on the 15th of August, 1991 -- I made a slip of the tongue. I'm sorry. The actual date is the 15th of August, 1991. In Beli Manastir, Ilija Djurkovic was assassinated and Neda Tomic from Karanac. Djurkovic died a few days later. This is something that all of Baranja knew about. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: I don't remember that. As for Karanac and Beli Manastir, I don't know anybody there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 17th of August, a Serb had been killed? His last name was Zivanovic, and the murderers took his body to Osijek, and this was something that was well-known in Baranja at the time as well.

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 19th of August, Ljubisa Kovacevic was killed? He was a driver, an ambulance driver from the medical centre in Darda.

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 21st of August at the cattle feed factory Zeljko Negovanovic, a worker, a Serb, was killed? Did you hear of that killing?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: I really don't know anyone, and I would not remember the name of someone who was killed from a neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just giving you a few examples and asking you about that. Were those perhaps the reasons why Serb women and children were leaving Baranja, this series of killings that was taking place precisely in the month of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: I know that most of our people left in August, and who killed who, I don't know. I just know what happened in my village of Grabovac and how many people were killed there. As for foreign villages, I don't remember names from there, and I wasn't informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 4, you say that Serbs in the second half of August of 1991 took over Baranja and held it under their control.

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes. It was like SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that on the 19th of August there was an attack by Croat forces precisely at the TO headquarters at Beli Manastir and that there was an armed conflict then?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: I don't know the exact dates. I cannot tell you that. I just know that it was very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any rate, your husband was not a member of the National Guards Corps or a politically active person; is that right, Mrs. Nadj?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: He was not. My husband was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, because these events you're testifying about pertain to December --

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that on the 30th of November, 1991, between Bajansko Selo [phoen] and Torjanci, a terrorist group of Croatian forces was infiltrated and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The witness can't help you about that. She can help about her own village, she says. No point going on about these other places.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that your husband was first arrested on the 4th of December, 1991, at 8.00 in the morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that he was taken then to the local commune building in Grabovac and that he returned from there the following day, if I understood correctly.

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Correct. Not only my husband but also many of them from the village were taken there and beaten up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband tell you then - I assume he did - who it was who arrested him and beat him then?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: I said that there was this captain who kept putting questions to him all the time. "You're a Hungarian. What do you have to do with Croatia?" But he did not introduce himself to my husband, and my husband did not have the right to ask, "Who are you?" He just knew it was some kind of captain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in Grabovac was there a JNA unit, any JNA unit, any JNA barracks, a JNA facility, something?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Well, they moved into empty houses and that's where they were, and then in the fields they had buried their tanks and that's where the army was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did your husband tell you the name of this captain?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: No, no. He did not introduce himself to my husband. He just -- he just kept saying, "You're a Hungarian. What have you got to do with the Croats?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mrs. Nadj. Do you know that Baranja as a whole was under the control of the Territorial Defence which consisted of the local population of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Well, probably, because it had been occupied, and the Yugoslav army came, and the local Serbs were all in uniform and now how you mean this was -- I mean, I don't really understand this. I can't follow it. Our people were no longer in the village. Very few had stayed behind. Very few of us had stayed behind. All the others had left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Your husband was arrested again on the 4th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Correct. And five others with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in April, that is to say a month before this event happened, that in the Baranja region another terrorist group was infiltrated?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that a breakthrough at Torjanci was attempted in which 2.500 members of the Croatian National Guards Corps took part?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: I am aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were commanded by Djuro Decak.

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: I don't know who was in command. All I know is that the Kotor people wanted to pass through and cross over but they didn't succeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that on that occasion quite a number of people were killed?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, as in paragraph 6, you describe the people who arrested your husband for the second time and say that one was wearing some sort of camouflage, masked uniform, and the other one was wearing civilian clothing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what would you say? Who could that man wearing the uniform have been, a Serb or perhaps a member of the forces who stormed Baranja during that time from the territory under Croatian control?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: I assume it must have been a Serb, because had it been anybody else, our people wouldn't have been taken off, old women and the others who never did any harm to anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that already in August you would see the local Serbs walking around with weapons and in uniforms going through your village and the surrounding parts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes, we did see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was it quite clear then that this man on the 4th of May need not have been a member of the JNA, but he might perhaps have been a member of some other formation, the one that came by with two civilians?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Well, I can't say one way or another whether he was a Serb or from SAO Krajina, the Serbs who stayed at home, but he was a Serb quite certainly, because had he not been a Serb, my husband would not have been killed and not killed in the way he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then I won't ask you any more questions about that, although I have a lot of information about the killings committed by the forces which stormed Baranja. Now, you say that they came to fetch your husband in a white minivan.

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any markings on the van?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Well, it was quite dark, and I was far too scared, because my husband had already been beaten a great deal in 1991, and I thought they were taking him off to be interrogated and that they would bring him back. And it was dark when the van turned up, so I wasn't really conscious of what was going on. I couldn't see the licence plates or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but it was quite clear that it wasn't a military vehicle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: No, it was not a military vehicle. It was not an army vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, you say that several days later, somebody told you that your husband was in a prison in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's the rumour that went round, that he was in a prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Well, people, the women told me that I should go to the prison because he was probably in prison. So I went to Beli Manastir to the prison there to take him a change of clothing and they said he wasn't there. And then I never heard anything else about him until I found him dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was six years later.

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it true that the prison was in the basement of the police station used by the police of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Well, it was over there away out of Beli Manastir. It was a building - I don't know what kind of building it was - I was there for the first time. This was a large building and I came into the building and said who I was looking for, and the man said that my husband wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I don't want to mention the man because I don't know whether he's protected or not, but is it true that a man, a son-in-law of a friend of yours who was a JNA officer, tried to learn your husband's whereabouts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what you say, he as a JNA officer was not able to find out the whereabouts of your husband either?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes. He looked for my husband and the five other men, but he couldn't find out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes. And he was looking for his mother-in-law, but he didn't learn anything, and then allegedly he went back to Belgrade and came back in a uniform. And then he went again and didn't learn anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he wasn't able to learn anything despite the fact that he was a JNA officer. Now, do you know who killed your husband at all?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what the circumstances of his death were?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: I really don't know. I can't tell you who killed my husband. All I do know is that our Baranja was occupied at the time and there were soldiers there and nobody else could have hit upon them than the Serbs. They are the only ones who could have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody talk to the nice couple whom you say were your neighbours and who had to have known who took your husband away?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: Yes. They went to the headquarters. We were very good -- on very good terms until the war broke out. When the war did break out, then we -- they thought of us as Ustashas, and to this day we're not on speaking terms. So I assume that he and this man Puskovic would have to know who took my husband off, because he was at the entrance and he had to -- he was the one letting vehicles enter and leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But just tell me this: The people from the police, the local police, later on who came, what Mr. McKeon asked you in closed session, when they came to ask you who took your husband away, did you tell them about your neighbours and say that your neighbours probably knew something about it?

utterances.speaker: BARBARA NADJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't send them on to my neighbours because I was afraid of this man Sosa. I was very much afraid, because wherever Sosa was, people were beaten up. And when we heard of Sosa, if you heard of Sosa being around, the best thing you could do was to hide and keep quiet. So we didn't dare ask anything or give any answers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Nadj. I'm not going to ask any more questions, no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no questions for Mrs. Nadj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: No redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Nadj, that concludes your evidence, and you are now free to go. Just take the time to compose yourself. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. Unless there is any matter. It may be convenient to adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is a short administrative matter I want to raise. Nothing to do with this witness. To save time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Nadj, would you like to go now? Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the Court's leave, we will be calling Stjepan Kljuc first thing tomorrow morning. He's a witness Your Honour certainly may be familiar with from an earlier case, a member of the Bosnian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Presidency for various periods. And I'm concerned to take his evidence concisely, and I'm concerned to save the accused's time in preparation. Out of an abundance of caution, before Mr. Kljuc arrived here, we served or, rather, re-served all the exhibits that -- we re-served all the exhibits that we thought he might relate to. That was a large quantity, I think it was re-served electronically, but nevertheless it was a large quantity. And so the first thing I'd like to do is to save the accused time by identifying a very much reduced list of exhibits that it's forecast at most the witness will deal with tomorrow. So that's one document I can make available to him and to Mr. Tapuskovic straight away in order to save time. A similar document is available for the Court. The witness will also be able to identify several intercepts. Now, I know handling intercepts is something that can be done very economically so far as time is concerned or it can take a large amount of time. What we've done, and we hope this is helpful, is to reflect the practice that you permitted when Dr. Williams produced a number of documentary exhibits, and we produce two charts, one relating to intercepts generally and one relating to Sarajevo-connected intercepts, which identify the voices that have been listened to, the relevant exhibit numbers, and commentary by Mr. Kljuc in rather the same way as Mr. Williams' chart produced commentary. I'm afraid I'm not a position at the moment to provide the transcripts of the intercepts themselves - they're all in the last stages of copying, translation, and so on - but we are at the moment able to provide, in case it should help, draft versions in English of the two charts dealing with intercepts and of the exhibit list. And if arrangements can be made to collect the other material later this afternoon so far as the accused is concerned, that should be available for him not too late, a couple of hours or so. I hope that that will make better use of our time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a witness you want to finish within the day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will, of course, partly depend on the length of the examination-in-chief which will then no doubt be reflected in the length of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have every intention to be rapid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must deal too tomorrow, possibly in the last session, with the fairly large number of witness statements who you've described as a priority that Mr. Groome has. We ought to deal with them, so time must be allowed, at least quarter of an hour or 20 minutes for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of July, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
